questions.q: x and y are real numbers and (2x − y) + (x + y)i = 4 + 5i. What are x and y?
questions.x: Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts: 2x − y = 4 and x + y = 5. Adding gives 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 2. Check: 6 − 2 = 4 and 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.q: Writing complex numbers as ordered pairs, what is (3, −2) + (−1, 5)?
questions.x: Ordered pairs add component by component: (3 + (−1), −2 + 5) = (2, 3). In the usual form this is (3 − 2i) + (−1 + 5i) = 2 + 3i.

questions.q: What is the value of 1/log₂6 + 1/log₃6?
questions.x: 1/log_a b = log_b a, so the sum is log₆2 + log₆3 = log₆6 = 1. Adding the bases 2 + 3 is the slip behind 5 and log₆5.

questions.q: Which point lies on the graph of y = ∛(x − 1) + 2?
questions.x: At x = 9, ∛(9 − 1) = ∛8 = 2, so y = 4. The graph is y = ∛x moved 1 unit right and 2 up, so it passes through (1, 2), not (1, 3); at x = −7 it gives ∛(−8) + 2 = 0, and at x = 2 it gives 3.

questions.q: lim(x→0) (x cos x)/(sin x) equals:
questions.x: (x cos x)/(sin x) = cos x · x/(sin x). As x → 0, cos x → 1 and x/(sin x) → 1, so the limit is 1.

questions.q: In the system AX = B, the coefficient matrix A is non-singular. What can be said about the system?
o: it has a solution only if B = O
it has the unique solution X = A⁻¹B
questions.x: |A| ≠ 0, so A⁻¹ exists, and multiplying AX = B on the left by A⁻¹ gives X = A⁻¹B, the only solution. No solution or infinitely many solutions can happen only when |A| = 0.

questions.q: The parabola y = x² + px + q cuts the x-axis at x = −1 and x = 5. What is the minimum value of y?
questions.x: y = (x + 1)(x − 5). The axis is halfway between the roots, at x = 2, so the minimum is (3)(−3) = −9. Check: y = x² − 4x − 5 = (x − 2)² − 9. Reading the constant term −5 as the minimum gives −5.

questions.q: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c opens downward and cuts the x-axis at one positive and one negative value of x. Which is true?
questions.x: Opening downward means a < 0. Roots of opposite signs have a negative product, so c/a < 0, and with a < 0 this gives c > 0. Check: y = −x² + 1 opens down, has roots ±1 and c = 1 > 0.

questions.q: Express (x² + 3)/(x² + 1)² in partial fractions.
questions.x: Write the numerator in terms of x² + 1: x² + 3 = (x² + 1) + 2. Dividing by (x² + 1)² gives 1/(x² + 1) + 2/(x² + 1)². Check at x = 0: 3/1 = 1 + 2. Keeping the 3 without taking 1 out gives the second form.

questions.q: An infinite geometric series has first term 5 and sum 15. What is its common ratio?
questions.x: S = a/(1 − r) gives 15 = 5/(1 − r), so 1 − r = 1/3 and r = 2/3. Check: 5/(1/3) = 15. Taking 1 − r = 2/3 gives 1/3, and r = 3 has no sum to infinity.

questions.q: In how many ways can 3 boys and 3 girls stand in a row so that boys and girls alternate?
questions.x: The pattern is either BGBGBG or GBGBGB (2 ways). In each, the boys can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways and the girls in 3! = 6 ways: 2 × 6 × 6 = 72. Forgetting that the row may start with a girl gives 36.

questions.q: For which positive integer n is (n + 1)! = 20 × (n − 1)!?
questions.x: (n + 1)! = (n + 1)n(n − 1)!, so n(n + 1) = 20 and n = 4 (the other root −5 is not allowed). Check: 5! = 120 and 20 × 3! = 120. Solving n + 1 = 20 gives 19.

questions.q: For |x| < 1, the coefficient of x² in the expansion of √(1 + x)/(1 − x) is:
questions.x: √(1 + x) = 1 + x/2 − x²/8 + … and 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + … . The x² terms give 1 + 1/2 − 1/8 = 11/8. Taking +x²/8 gives 13/8, and dropping the x² term of the root gives 3/2.

questions.q: What is the value of cos 300°?
questions.x: 300° = 360° − 60° lies in the fourth quadrant, where cosine is positive, so cos 300° = cos 60° = 1/2. Taking the fourth-quadrant sign as negative gives −1/2.

questions.q: Given tan(α + π/4) = 3, what is tan α?
questions.x: tan(α + π/4) = (tan α + 1)/(1 − tan α) = 3, so tan α + 1 = 3 − 3 tan α and tan α = 1/2. Check: (1/2 + 1)/(1 − 1/2) = 3. Using 1 + tan α in the denominator gives 2.

questions.q: What is the range of y = cot x?
questions.x: On (0, π), cot x = cos x/sin x falls from +∞ to −∞ without a break, so it takes every real value. [−1, 1] is the range of sin and cos, and (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞) is that of sec and cosec.

questions.q: In any triangle ABC, the law of tangents states that (a − b)/(a + b) equals:
questions.x: From a/b = sin A/sin B, (a − b)/(a + b) = (sin A − sin B)/(sin A + sin B) = [2 cos((A + B)/2) sin((A − B)/2)]/[2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2)] = tan((A − B)/2)/tan((A + B)/2). The inverted form gives (a + b)/(a − b).

questions.q: Which statement about principal values is true?
questions.x: cos⁻¹ takes values in [0, π] and cos π = −1, so cos⁻¹(−1) = π. The others leave the principal range or use the wrong angle: sin⁻¹(−1) = −π/2, tan⁻¹(−√3) = −π/3, cos⁻¹(0) = π/2.

questions.q: The general solution of cos θ = 0 is (n ∈ Z):
questions.x: cos θ = 0 at π/2 and 3π/2 in one turn, which are π apart, so θ = π/2 + nπ. θ = π/2 + 2nπ misses 3π/2, and θ = nπ solves sin θ = 0.

questions.q: For f(x) = 1/(x + 1), what does the difference quotient [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h simplify to (h ≠ 0)?
questions.x: 1/(x + h + 1) − 1/(x + 1) = (x + 1 − x − h − 1)/((x + h + 1)(x + 1)) = −h/((x + h + 1)(x + 1)); dividing by h gives −1/((x + h + 1)(x + 1)). Only after h → 0 does it become −1/(x + 1)².

questions.q: In the Maclaurin series of 1/(1 − x)², what is the coefficient of x³?
questions.x: 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + x⁴ + ...; differentiating gives 1/(1 − x)² = 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³ + ..., so the coefficient is 4. Check: f‴(0)/3! = 24/6 = 4, since f‴(x) = 24/(1 − x)⁵.

questions.q: ∫ sec²x dx equals:
questions.x: Since d/dx tan x = sec²x, the antiderivative is tan x + C. −cot x + C is the antiderivative of cosec²x, and sec x tan x is the derivative of sec x.

questions.q: For a function f with a continuous second derivative, ∫ x f″(x) dx equals:
questions.x: Parts with u = x, dv = f″(x) dx, v = f′(x): x f′(x) − ∫f′(x) dx = x f′(x) − f(x) + C. Check: d/dx[x f′ − f] = f′ + x f″ − f′ = x f″.

questions.q: What are the order and degree of the differential equation d²y/dx² + sin(dy/dx) = 0?
questions.x: The highest derivative is d²y/dx², so the order is 2. The equation is not a polynomial in the derivatives (dy/dx sits inside sine), so its degree is not defined. Reading degree 1 from the power of d²y/dx² is the usual slip.

questions.q: What is the perimeter of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (3, 0) and (0, 4)?
questions.x: The sides are 3, 4 and √(3² + 4²) = 5, so the perimeter is 12. 6 is the area, not the perimeter.

questions.q: A line passes through (0, 2) and makes an angle of 135° with the positive x-axis. What is its equation?
questions.x: Slope = tan 135° = −1, so y = −x + 2, i.e. x + y − 2 = 0. Taking tan 135° = 1 gives x − y + 2 = 0.

questions.q: What is the acute angle between the asymptotes of the hyperbola x²/3 − y² = 1?
questions.x: The asymptotes are y = ±x/√3, each making 30° with the x-axis, so the acute angle between them is 60°. 30° is only the angle each makes with the axis.

questions.q: What is the equation of the normal to the parabola y² = 4x at the point (1, 2)?
questions.x: 2y·y′ = 4 gives y′ = 2/y = 1 at (1, 2), so the normal has slope −1: y − 2 = −(x − 1), i.e. x + y − 3 = 0. x − y + 1 = 0 is the tangent there.

questions.q: For r(t) = cos t i + sin t j + t k, what is d/dt(|r(t)|²)?
questions.x: |r|² = cos²t + sin²t + t² = 1 + t², whose derivative is 2t. Check: 2r · r′ = 2(−cos t sin t + sin t cos t + t) = 2t.

questions.q: What is the distance between the points A(1, −2, 3) and B(3, 1, −3)?
questions.x: AB = 2i + 3j − 6k, so |AB| = √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7. Leaving out the z-part gives √13.

questions.q: The true value of g is 9.8 m s⁻². A student's five readings are 8.52, 8.51, 8.53, 8.52 and 8.52 m s⁻². These readings are:
questions.x: The readings agree closely with one another (spread about 0.01 m s⁻²), so they are precise, but all lie far from 9.8 m s⁻², so they are not accurate; a systematic error is likely. Mixing up the two words gives the reverse answer.

questions.q: Four students record the length of the same rod. Which recorded value was measured with the greatest precision?
questions.x: Precision depends on the smallest division (absolute uncertainty) of the instrument; 12.346 cm is recorded to 0.001 cm, the finest of the four. 12 cm, to the nearest centimetre, is the least precise.

questions.q: The unit vector in the direction of the vector 3î + 4ĵ is:
questions.x: Magnitude = √(3² + 4²) = 5, so the unit vector is (3î + 4ĵ)/5 = 0.6î + 0.8ĵ; check: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1. Dividing by 3 + 4 = 7 instead of the magnitude is the common slip.

questions.q: A stone dropped from rest from a height h takes time t to reach the ground. Ignoring air resistance, a stone dropped from a height 4h takes:
questions.x: h = ½gt², so t ∝ √h; four times the height gives √4 = 2 times the time. Taking t ∝ h gives 4t.

questions.q: A 3 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is tied by a light string, passing over a smooth pulley at the table's edge, to a 2 kg mass hanging freely. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the tension in the string is:
questions.x: Only the hanging weight drives both: a = 20/(3 + 2) = 4 m s⁻²; the string accelerates the 3 kg block, so T = 3 × 4 = 12 N. Check on the hanging mass: 20 − T = 2 × 4, so T = 12 N. Taking T equal to the weight, 20 N, ignores the acceleration.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car climbs a straight slope that rises 1 m for every 20 m along the road (sin θ = 1/20) at a steady 10 m s⁻¹. The resistive forces total 500 N. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the power of the engine is:
questions.x: Driving force = mg sin θ + resistance = 1000 × 10/20 + 500 = 1000 N; P = Fv = 1000 × 10 = 10 kW. Check: per second it lifts 1000 kg by 0.5 m (5 kW) and works 500 N over 10 m (5 kW). Forgetting either part gives 5 kW; using the full weight gives 105 kW.

questions.q: A geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the Earth's surface. Its orbit must be:
o: In the equatorial plane, moving from east to west
In the equatorial plane, moving from west to east
A polar orbit, passing over both poles
In any plane through the Earth's centre, moving from west to east
questions.x: To stay over one point it must turn with the Earth: the same 24 h period, the same sense of rotation (west to east) and an orbit in the equatorial plane. An orbit in any other plane would carry it north and south of the equator during each day.

questions.q: A satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface has a speed of 8 km s⁻¹. Another satellite orbits at a height above the surface equal to the Earth's radius. Its orbital speed is:
questions.x: The second orbit has radius R + R = 2R, and v = √(GM/r) ∝ 1/√r, so v = 8/√2 = 4√2 ≈ 5.7 km s⁻¹. Taking v ∝ 1/r gives 4 km s⁻¹; forgetting that a higher orbit is slower gives 8√2.

questions.q: The viscosity of a fluid is a measure of:
o: The upward force it exerts on a body immersed in it
The frictional resistance between its layers as they slide past one another
The pressure it exerts on the walls of its container
The attraction between its molecules and a solid surface
questions.x: Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid: the resistance of one layer sliding over the next. The upward force on an immersed body is the upthrust, which belongs to Archimedes' principle.

questions.q: A mass–spring system has period T when it oscillates horizontally on a smooth table. When the same mass hangs from the same spring and oscillates vertically, its period is:
questions.x: T = 2π√(m/k) depends only on the mass and the spring constant, not on g. Gravity only shifts the mean position downward by mg/k, so the period is still T.

questions.q: A 500 Hz tuning fork is held over a tube closed at its lower end. Resonance is heard when the air column is 17 cm long and again when it is 51 cm long. Ignoring end correction, the speed of sound is:
questions.x: Successive resonances in a closed tube differ by λ/2: 51 − 17 = 34 cm, so λ = 68 cm and v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹ (check: the first resonance L = λ/4 = 17 cm). Taking 34 cm as λ gives 170 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A glass lens of refractive index 1.5 is coated with a thin film of refractive index 1.25. Light of wavelength 500 nm (in air) falls on it normally. What is the smallest film thickness for which the light reflected from the two surfaces of the film cancels?
questions.x: Both reflections (air to film, film to glass) are from a rarer to a denser medium, so both get a phase change of π and these cancel. Cancellation then needs 2nt = λ/2, so t = λ/(4n) = 500/(4 × 1.25) = 100 nm. Counting a phase change at only one surface gives 2nt = λ and 200 nm.

questions.q: Light whose wavefronts are 600 nm apart (one cycle apart) in air enters water of refractive index 4/3. How far apart are the wavefronts, one cycle apart, in the water?
questions.x: The frequency is unchanged and the speed falls by the factor n, so λ in water = 600/(4/3) = 450 nm. Multiplying by n instead of dividing gives 800 nm.

questions.q: A telescope objective of diameter 12.2 cm is used with light of wavelength 600 nm. Using α = 1.22 λ/D, what is the smallest distance between two craters on the Moon, 4 × 10⁸ m away, that it can just resolve?
questions.x: α = 1.22 × 6 × 10⁻⁷/0.122 = 6 × 10⁻⁶ rad. Separation = α × distance = 6 × 10⁻⁶ × 4 × 10⁸ = 2.4 × 10³ m = 2.4 km. Leaving out the factor 1.22 gives about 2.0 km; taking D as 1.22 cm gives 24 km.

questions.q: Four gas molecules have speeds of 100, 500, 500 and 700 m s⁻¹. What is their root-mean-square speed?
questions.x: Mean of squares = (1 + 25 + 25 + 49) × 10⁴/4 = 25 × 10⁴ m² s⁻², so v(rms) = 500 m s⁻¹. The ordinary mean speed is 1800/4 = 450 m s⁻¹, which is the tempting slip.

questions.q: Charges of +9 μC and −1 μC are fixed 20 cm apart. Where on the line through them would a small third charge feel zero net force?
o: 5 cm from the −1 μC charge, between the two charges
10 cm from the −1 μC charge, on the side away from the +9 μC charge
15 cm from the +9 μC charge, between the two charges
10 cm from the +9 μC charge, on the side away from the −1 μC charge
questions.x: Between unlike charges both forces on a test charge point the same way, so the point lies outside, nearer the smaller charge. 9/(x + 20)² = 1/x² gives 3x = x + 20, x = 10 cm beyond the −1 μC charge. Check: 9/30² = 1/10² = 0.01.

questions.q: Two identical small conducting spheres carry charges of +6 μC and −2 μC and attract each other with force F. They are touched together and then returned to the same separation. The force between them now is:
questions.x: On touching, the total charge +4 μC is shared equally: +2 μC each. Before, |q₁q₂| = 12; after, 4. So the force is F/3, and since both are now positive it is repulsive.

questions.q: Capacitors of 2 μF and 4 μF are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. The total charge they store is:
questions.x: In parallel C = 2 + 4 = 6 μF, so Q = CV = 6 × 12 = 72 μC. Taking them in series (4/3 μF) gives 16 μC.

questions.q: A graph of current (vertical axis) against p.d. (horizontal axis) for a filament lamp curves over and bends towards the p.d. axis as the p.d. increases. This shows that the lamp's resistance:
o: Increases, because the filament gets hotter
Decreases, because the filament gets hotter
Stays constant, as for any metal
Falls to zero at high p.d.
questions.x: R = V/I, and on this graph each step in V gives a smaller rise in I, so V/I grows. The hotter filament has more vibrating ions, so its resistance rises. A falling resistance would make the curve bend towards the current axis.

questions.q: A flat coil of area 0.2 m² is in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field. The magnetic flux through the coil is (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87):
questions.x: Φ = BA cos θ with θ the angle between B and the normal to the coil. The plane is at 30° to B, so the normal is at 60°: Φ = 0.5 × 0.2 × cos 60° = 0.05 Wb. Using cos 30° (the angle with the plane) gives 0.087 Wb.

questions.q: A rectangular loop of wire carrying a steady current is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The net magnetic force on the whole loop is:
o: Zero, although the loop may experience a torque
Largest when the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field
Equal to BIL for each side, added together
questions.x: In a uniform field the forces on opposite sides of a closed loop are equal and opposite, so they add to zero. They can still form a couple, which is why a coil turns in a motor or meter.

questions.q: For an ideal transformer, which quantity is the same for the primary and the secondary?
questions.x: An ideal transformer has no losses, so VpIp = VsIs: the power in equals the power out. Voltage and current change in opposite ratios set by the turns ratio.

questions.q: A choke (a coil of large inductance and small resistance) is used instead of a resistor to limit the alternating current in a fluorescent tube circuit, because the choke:
o: Has a very high resistance to AC
Increases the voltage across the tube at all times
Wastes very little energy as heat
questions.x: A choke limits current through its reactance; in an ideal inductor the average power over a cycle is zero, so little energy is lost as heat. A resistor limiting the same current would waste I²R continuously.

questions.q: Trivalent impurity atoms such as gallium, added to pure germanium to make a p-type semiconductor, are called acceptor atoms because each one:
o: Accepts a hole and releases a free electron
Accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, creating a hole
Accepts a proton from the germanium nucleus
Accepts energy and becomes an insulator
questions.x: A trivalent atom forms only three of the four covalent bonds; it takes an electron from a neighbouring bond to complete the fourth, which leaves a hole that can move. Pentavalent atoms do the opposite: they donate a free electron (donors).

questions.q: A p-n junction is kept at a fixed reverse bias, well below breakdown, while its temperature is raised. Its reverse current:
o: Decreases, because the depletion region becomes wider
Increases, because more minority carriers are produced thermally
Stays exactly the same, as it depends only on the voltage
questions.x: The reverse current is due to minority carriers, which are created by thermal breaking of bonds; heating produces more of them, so the reverse current rises. A fixed bias does not widen the depletion region further, so the current does not fall.

questions.q: A passenger in a train moving along a straight track at constant velocity drops a ball. Ignoring air resistance, the passenger and an observer standing beside the track see the ball's path as:
o: A parabola for the passenger and a vertical straight line for the observer
A vertical straight line for the passenger and a parabola for the observer
A vertical straight line for both
questions.x: In the train's inertial frame the ball starts with zero horizontal velocity, so it falls straight down. On the ground it also has the train's horizontal velocity, so it follows a projectile's parabola. Both observers agree on the laws of motion, only the description differs.

questions.q: Photoelectrons are emitted almost instantly (within about 10⁻⁹ s) even when very dim light of suitable frequency falls on a metal. This observation supports the idea that:
o: Light energy is spread evenly over the wave front
Electrons need time to collect energy from the light wave
Light energy arrives in packets (photons), each absorbed by a single electron
The work function falls when light is dim
questions.x: In wave theory dim light would need time for an electron to collect enough energy; in the photon picture a single photon gives all its energy hf to one electron at once, so emission is immediate. The work function is a property of the metal, not of the light.

questions.q: A large number of hydrogen atoms are all excited to the level n = 4. As they return to the ground state by every possible route, the number of different spectral lines that can be emitted is:
questions.x: The possible transitions are 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1, which is n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6. Counting only the direct jumps from n = 4 gives 3; 10 is the count for n = 5.

questions.q: In Rutherford's scattering experiment, a very small number of alpha particles were turned back through angles greater than 90°. This showed that:
o: Electrons are much heavier than alpha particles
The positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
The atom is mostly empty space
Alpha particles are attracted by gold atoms
questions.x: Only a very strong repulsion from a small, massive, positive centre can turn a fast, heavy alpha particle back; the rarity of such events shows the nucleus is tiny. 'Mostly empty space' comes from the particles that went straight through, not from the back-scattered ones.

questions.q: The fundamental force responsible for the β-decay of a radioactive nucleus is the:
questions.x: β-decay changes one quark flavour into another (for example d → u), which only the weak force, carried by W bosons, can do. The strong force holds quarks and nucleons together but does not change flavours.

questions.q: 2.4 g of magnesium is added to a solution containing 0.15 mol of HCl: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What volume of hydrogen, measured at STP, is formed? (Mg = 24; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: Mg = 0.1 mol needs 0.2 mol HCl, but only 0.15 mol is present, so HCl is limiting. H₂ = 0.15/2 = 0.075 mol = 0.075 × 22.4 = 1.68 dm³. Working from Mg (the excess reactant) gives 2.24 dm³; ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio gives 3.36 dm³.

questions.q: The actual yield of a product is usually less than its theoretical yield mainly because:
o: The excess reactant is left unreacted at the end
Some product is lost during separation and purification, or side reactions occur
Mass is destroyed during the chemical reaction
The theoretical yield is always calculated from the excess reactant
questions.x: Losses while filtering, transferring and purifying, and side reactions giving other products, reduce the amount actually collected. A leftover excess reactant is normal and does not lower the yield; mass is conserved; and the theoretical yield is worked out from the limiting reactant.

questions.q: A gas occupies 400 cm³ at 27 °C and 1 atm. What volume will it occupy at 177 °C and 2 atm?
questions.x: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 400 × (1/2) × (450/300) = 300 cm³. Ignoring the temperature gives 200 cm³, and using °C instead of K (177/27) gives about 1311 cm³.

questions.q: Which order of boiling points is correct?
questions.x: All three hydrogen-bond. Water forms two hydrogen bonds per molecule (two H and two lone pairs), building a 3D network, so it boils highest (100 °C); HF boils at about 20 °C and NH₃ at about −33 °C. Ranking by electronegativity alone puts HF on top.

questions.q: Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom gives a line in the infrared region of the spectrum?
questions.x: Lines ending at n = 3 form the Paschen series, in the infrared. Transitions ending at n = 2 (Balmer) are visible and those ending at n = 1 (Lyman) are ultraviolet; judging by the starting level instead of the final level is the slip.

questions.q: A period 4 element has three unpaired electrons, all in its 4p subshell, in the ground state. Its atomic number and group are:
questions.x: Three unpaired 4p electrons means 4p³: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³, Z = 18 + 10 + 2 + 3 = 33 (arsenic), with 5 valence electrons, group VA. Counting only the p electrons gives group IIIA; 23 (vanadium) has its unpaired electrons in 3d, and 15 is phosphorus in period 3.

questions.q: What is the hybridisation of boron in BF₃ and of nitrogen in NH₃?
questions.x: Boron forms three σ bonds and has no lone pair: three hybrid orbitals, sp², planar. Nitrogen forms three σ bonds and also has a lone pair: four regions, sp³, pyramidal. Giving both sp² comes from counting only the bonds and forgetting nitrogen's lone pair.

questions.q: Standard enthalpies of formation in kJ mol⁻¹: C₂H₅OH(l) −278, CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(l) −286. What is the standard enthalpy of combustion of ethanol, C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)?
questions.x: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = [2(−394) + 3(−286)] − (−278) = −1646 + 278 = −1368 kJ mol⁻¹ (O₂ is zero). −1646 forgets the reactant term; −1924 adds it with the wrong sign; −1082 uses 2 instead of 3 mol of water.

questions.q: 1.0 mol of CO(g) and 1.0 mol of H₂O(g) are heated in a closed 1.0 dm³ vessel: CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g). Kc = 4.0 at this temperature. How many moles of CO₂ are present at equilibrium?
questions.x: If x mol react, Kc = x² / (1 − x)² = 4.0, so x / (1 − x) = 2 and x = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 mol. Forgetting to take the square root, x / (1 − x) = 4, gives 0.80; 0.33 is the CO left over, not the CO₂ formed.

questions.q: What is the Kc expression for the heterogeneous equilibrium CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)?
questions.x: The concentrations of pure solids are constant and are taken into the value of K, so only the gas appears: Kc = [CO₂]. Writing in the solids follows the general formula without that rule.

questions.q: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide solution?
o: Methyl orange, because the end point is below pH 7
Phenolphthalein, because the end point is above pH 7
Methyl orange, because ethanoic acid is weak
Either indicator, because the end point is exactly pH 7
questions.x: At the end point the solution contains CH₃COONa, which is hydrolysed and basic (pH about 8–9). Phenolphthalein changes colour over about pH 8.3–10, which matches; methyl orange changes at about pH 3–4.5 and would change too early. 'Exactly pH 7' is true only for a strong acid with a strong base.

questions.q: What mass of copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, is needed to make 500 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CuSO₄ solution? (Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.x: Moles needed = 0.10 × 0.500 = 0.050 mol. Molar mass of CuSO₄·5H₂O = 63.5 + 32 + 64 + 90 = 249.5 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.050 × 249.5 ≈ 12.5 g. Using anhydrous CuSO₄ (159.5 g mol⁻¹) gives 8.0 g; forgetting the 500 cm³ gives 25.0 g.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇?
questions.x: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = 12, so x = +6. +12 is the total for both chromium atoms, not the value for one.

questions.q: For an endothermic reaction, which statement must be true?
o: The activation energy of the forward reaction is greater than that of the reverse reaction
The activation energy of the forward reaction is less than ΔH
The reverse reaction has no activation energy
A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy but not the reverse one
questions.x: Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse) = ΔH, which is positive for an endothermic reaction, so Ea(forward) is larger. Ea(forward) can never be less than ΔH, and a catalyst lowers both activation energies by the same amount.

questions.q: Which of these period 3 oxides has the highest melting point?
questions.x: MgO is a giant ionic lattice of doubly charged ions (Mg²⁺, O²⁻), so its lattice is very strong (melting point about 2850 °C). Na₂O has singly charged Na⁺, so it melts lower; P₄O₁₀ and SO₃ are molecular and melt or sublime at low temperatures.

questions.q: Lithium has the most negative standard electrode potential of the alkali metals, even though its first ionisation energy is the highest in the group. The main reason is that:
o: Lithium has the largest atoms in the group
The very small Li⁺ ion has a very large hydration energy
Lithium has the lowest melting point in the group
Li⁺ ions are not hydrated in water
questions.x: The electrode potential reflects the whole change M(s) → M⁺(aq). The small Li⁺ ion is very strongly hydrated, and this large release of energy outweighs its higher ionisation energy. Lithium has the smallest atoms and the highest melting point in the group.

questions.q: Borax reacts with hydrochloric acid: Na₂B₄O₇ + 2HCl + 5H₂O → 2NaCl + 4H₃BO₃. What volume of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ HCl reacts exactly with 3.82 g of borax, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O (molar mass 382 g mol⁻¹)?
questions.x: 3.82 / 382 = 0.010 mol borax, which needs 2 × 0.010 = 0.020 mol HCl; volume = 0.020 / 0.20 = 0.10 dm³ = 100 cm³. Ignoring the 1 : 2 mole ratio gives 50 cm³.

questions.q: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with charcoal. The products are:
questions.x: Hot concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as an oxidising agent: C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂ + 2SO₂ + 2H₂O, carbon going from 0 to +4 and sulphur from +6 to +4. Electron check: C loses 4 e⁻ and two S gain 2 e⁻ each. H₂S forms only with strong reducing agents, not carbon.

questions.q: Before testing a solution for halide ions with silver nitrate, it is acidified with dilute nitric acid. This is done to:
o: Make the silver halide precipitate dissolve
Oxidise the halide ions to the free halogen
Remove ions such as carbonate that would also give a precipitate with Ag⁺
Provide extra silver ions for the precipitate
questions.x: Carbonate (and hydroxide) ions would form Ag₂CO₃ or Ag₂O precipitates and give a false result; nitric acid destroys them and adds no halide ions itself. Dilute HNO₃ does not oxidise halide ions, so that option is wrong.

questions.q: Excess AgNO₃ solution is added to a solution containing 0.010 mol of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂. What mass of AgCl is precipitated? (AgCl = 143.5 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: Only the two chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are free in solution; the Cl bonded to cobalt is not precipitated. 0.020 mol AgCl × 143.5 = 2.87 g. Counting all three chlorines gives 0.030 mol, 4.31 g.

questions.q: How many chiral carbon atoms (each bonded to four different groups) are present in CH₃CH(OH)CH(Cl)CH₃?
questions.x: C-2 carries CH₃, OH, H and CH(Cl)CH₃, and C-3 carries CH₃, Cl, H and CH(OH)CH₃, so both are chiral; the end CH₃ carbons have three identical H atoms. Spotting only the carbon with OH gives 1.

questions.q: What mass of carbon dioxide is formed when 2.2 g of propane, C₃H₈, burns completely in excess oxygen? (C₃H₈ = 44, CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 2.2/44 = 0.05 mol propane gives 0.15 mol CO₂ = 6.6 g. Forgetting the 1:3 ratio gives 2.2 g; 3.6 g is the mass of water (0.20 mol × 18).

questions.q: Benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH, is brominated with Br₂ and FeBr₃. The main product is:
questions.x: –COOH withdraws electrons and is a meta director, so Br goes to position 3. Treating –COOH like –OH gives the ortho/para products; tribromination happens only with strongly activated rings such as phenol.

questions.q: 0.10 mol of ethylmagnesium bromide reacts completely with excess methanal, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. What mass of alcohol is obtained? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.x: C₂H₅MgBr + HCHO then H₃O⁺ gives CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, propan-1-ol (M = 60); 1:1 ratio, so 0.10 × 60 = 6.0 g. 4.6 g forgets that methanal adds a carbon and uses ethanol (46); 7.4 g uses a four-carbon alcohol.

questions.q: The –OH group makes the benzene ring of phenol much more reactive towards electrophiles than benzene. The reason is that:
o: Oxygen withdraws electrons from the ring by its high electronegativity
The –OH group makes the ring lose its delocalised π system
The hydrogen of –OH is transferred to the electrophile
A lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising the electron density at the ortho and para positions
questions.x: Resonance donation (+M) of an oxygen lone pair outweighs oxygen's inductive withdrawal, so the ring is activated, especially at ortho and para. Inductive withdrawal alone would deactivate the ring.

questions.q: When a nucleophile adds to the carbonyl group of an aldehyde, the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon changes:
questions.x: The C=O carbon has three σ bonds and a π bond (sp², 120°). After addition the π bond is gone and the carbon has four σ bonds (sp³, about 109.5°). The reverse change happens in elimination.

questions.q: Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid. The products are:
questions.x: Acid hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond: CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl, the ammonia being held as its salt. Sodium ethanoate and ammonia are the products of alkaline hydrolysis, the most tempting mix-up.

questions.q: Which conditions convert bromoethane mainly into ethene rather than ethanol?
o: Heating with concentrated KOH in ethanol
questions.x: In ethanol the hydroxide acts mainly as a base and removes HBr (elimination), giving CH₂=CH₂. In water the hydroxide acts mainly as a nucleophile and substitution gives ethanol, which is the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.x: RNA uses uracil in place of the thymine of DNA; adenine, guanine and cytosine are found in both. Choosing thymine reverses the two nucleic acids.

questions.q: In cement manufacture, the dry process uses less fuel than the wet process mainly because:
o: No water has to be evaporated from the raw mix in the kiln
The clinker is formed at a much lower temperature
No limestone has to be decomposed
Gypsum is added before the mix enters the kiln
questions.x: In the wet process the raw materials are fed as a slurry, and a lot of heat goes into boiling off the water; the dry process feeds powder. Both processes still decompose limestone and reach the same clinkering temperature, so those options are wrong.

questions.q: A hospital pays a software house to write a program designed only for its own patient-record system. Such software is called:
questions.x: Software written to order for one particular user or organisation is custom-built (tailor-made). Packaged software is ready-made and sold to many users, like a common word processor.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-impact printer?
questions.x: A laser printer forms the image with a laser and toner, with nothing striking the paper, so it is non-impact. Dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and drum line printers strike an inked ribbon against the paper, so they are impact printers.

questions.q: Saima is editing a large report. She saved it to the hard disk an hour ago and has made changes since. The power suddenly fails. What is lost?
o: The whole report, including the copy saved on the hard disk
Only the changes made since the last save, which were in RAM
Nothing, because RAM keeps data without power
Only the copy on the hard disk, while RAM keeps the changes
questions.x: Unsaved changes are held in volatile RAM and are lost, but the hard disk is non-volatile, so the version saved an hour ago remains. RAM does not keep data when power fails.

questions.q: Which list contains only guided (wired) transmission media?
o: Twisted-pair cable, coaxial cable, fibre-optic cable
questions.x: Guided media send signals along a physical path, which is true of twisted-pair, coaxial and fibre-optic cables. Microwave, infrared, radio, satellite and Bluetooth travel through air or space, so they are unguided.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches an OSI layer with the name of its data unit?
questions.x: The Network layer handles packets, the Data Link layer frames, the Transport layer segments, and the Physical layer raw bits. Frame and segment are swapped in two of the wrong pairs.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches each example with its transmission mode?
o: Radio broadcast: half-duplex; video call: simplex
Radio broadcast: full-duplex; video call: half-duplex
Radio broadcast: simplex; video call: full-duplex
Radio broadcast: simplex; video call: half-duplex
questions.x: A radio station only sends and listeners only receive, which is simplex; in a video call both people speak and hear at the same time, which is full-duplex. Half-duplex would force the callers to take turns, like a walkie-talkie.

questions.q: Someone removes the copy protection from a paid program so that it runs without a valid licence key. This is called:
questions.x: Cracking defeats a program's licence protection and is a form of software piracy. Debugging means finding and fixing errors in one's own code.

questions.q: Where should a backup of important files be kept so that it is still safe if the house suffers a fire or a theft?
o: In a different place, such as cloud storage or another building
In another folder on the same laptop
On a second partition of the same hard disk
On a USB drive kept next to the laptop
questions.x: A backup must be kept away from the original, off-site or in the cloud, so one disaster cannot destroy both. Another folder, partition or a USB next to the laptop would be lost along with it.

questions.q: Which job is normally done by batch processing rather than in real time?
o: Booking a seat on a train online
Printing the monthly electricity bills of all customers together
questions.x: Monthly bills can be collected and processed all at once, with no need for an instant reply, so they suit batch processing. An autopilot, a booking or an ATM withdrawal must respond immediately.

questions.q: A school's software does not teach lessons, but it records each student's test results, tracks progress and decides which lesson each student should study next. This is:
questions.x: Computer-managed instruction (also called computer-managed learning) manages records, testing and the order of lessons. CAI is the program that actually presents the lesson and questions to the student.

questions.q: The pieces of many files on a hard disk are scattered in different places, which slows down reading. Which Windows tool rearranges them so that each file's pieces are stored together?
questions.x: Defragmentation gathers the scattered parts of each file into neighbouring places on the disk, so the disk reads faster. Formatting would erase everything on the disk.

questions.q: In Excel, which part of the window shows the formula of the active cell, even when the cell itself shows only the result?
questions.x: The formula bar shows the actual contents of the selected cell, such as `=A1+B1`, while the cell shows its value. The sheet tab only shows the worksheet's name.

questions.q: In which data model can a child record be linked to more than one parent record, so that the records form a graph-like structure?
questions.x: The network model allows a record to have several parents, linked like a graph. The hierarchical model is a tree in which each child has exactly one parent.

questions.q: Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptName) is split into Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID) and Dept(DeptID, DeptName). Which of these becomes possible?
o: Storing the department name in every employee row
Giving two departments the same DeptID
Recording a new department before any employee joins it
Deleting a department that still has employees without any check
questions.x: A department can now be a row of Dept on its own, so the insertion anomaly is gone. Storing the name in every employee row is the redundancy the split removed.

questions.q: On a form, a text box bound to RollNo has an attached label that shows "RollNo". To make the label show "Roll Number", which property is changed?
o: The Control Source of the text box
The Record Source of the form
The Default Value of the text box
questions.x: A label's text is its Caption property. Changing the text box's Control Source would change which field it shows, not the words beside it.

questions.q: A table's ID field is AutoNumber. Records with IDs 1 to 5 were added, and then the record with ID 5 was deleted. The database has not been compacted. What ID does the next new record get?
questions.x: AutoNumber keeps counting from the last number it gave out and does not reuse a deleted number, so the next record gets 6. AutoNumber values are never typed by the user.

questions.q: Which header file must be included to use the library functions `sqrt()` and `pow()`?
questions.x: The mathematical functions such as sqrt() and pow() are declared in math.h. stdio.h declares input/output functions such as printf() and scanf().

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("[%2d]", 12345);
```
questions.x: A field width is a minimum: a number that needs more places is printed in full, so all five digits appear. The width never cuts digits off.
x is printed and then changed: 1 -> 3 -> 7 -> 15 -> 31. After 15 is printed x becomes 31, the test 31 < 20 fails and the loop ends, so 31 is never printed.
age < 12 is false because 12 is not less than 12, so the conditional operator gives 500 and fee = 1000 + 500 = 1500. 1200 comes from wrongly taking 12 < 12 as true.
Only the newline characters are counted, and each of the three lines ends with one, so n = 3. 11 counts the letters and 14 counts every character, letters and newlines together.

questions.q: Which is a correct `if-else` statement in C?
questions.x: In C the condition goes in brackets, there is no then keyword, and each simple statement ends with a semicolon. The colon form is Python-like and the then form is from other languages.

questions.q: In a Waterfall project, why does the client sign the requirements document before the design stage begins?
o: So that coding can begin before the design is drawn
So that no testing will be needed later
So that the requirements can be changed freely during coding
So both sides agree on what will be built before later stages depend on it
questions.x: Every later Waterfall stage is built on the requirements, so they are fixed and agreed first; a change later means going back through the stages. Signing does not replace design or testing.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print(grid[1][0] + grid[0][2])
```
questions.x: `grid[1]` is the second inner list [4, 5, 6], so `grid[1][0]` is 4; `grid[0][2]` is the third item of [1, 2, 3], which is 3. 4 + 3 = 7.
Subtraction works left to right: (10 − 4) − 3 = 3. `2 ** -1` is 1/2 = 0.5, and `9 ** 0.5` is the square root of 9 as a float, 3.0. 9 would come from 10 − (4 − 3).

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
d = {"pen": 3, "ink": 7}
print(list(d.keys()), sum(d.values()))
```
questions.x: `keys()` gives the keys, shown as the list ['pen', 'ink'], and `values()` gives 3 and 7, whose sum is 10. [3, 7] is the list of values, not keys.

questions.q: An undirected graph has edges P–Q, P–R, Q–S, R–S and S–T. A depth-first traversal starts at P; from each vertex it goes to the first unvisited neighbour in alphabetical order, and goes back only when there is none. In what order are the vertices visited?
questions.x: P → Q (first neighbour) → S (Q's only unvisited one) → R (S's first unvisited one); R has no unvisited neighbours, so go back to S → T. P, Q, R, S, T is the breadth-first order.

questions.q: Bubble sort (ascending) goes left to right and swaps each adjacent pair whose left value is larger. How many swaps does it make in the first full pass on `[4, 2, 5, 1, 3]`?
questions.x: 4 > 2 swap → [2, 4, 5, 1, 3]; 4 < 5 no swap; 5 > 1 swap → [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]; 5 > 3 swap → [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]. Three swaps; 4 is the number of comparisons, not swaps.

questions.q: A problem to which every problem in NP can be reduced in polynomial time, but which need not itself be in NP, is called:
questions.x: That is the definition of NP-hard. NP-complete problems are the NP-hard problems that are also in NP, so "need not be in NP" points to NP-hard.

questions.q: Every value in a data set is increased by 5. What happens to the mean and to the range?
o: The mean increases by 5; the range stays the same
The mean stays the same; the range increases by 5
questions.x: Adding 5 to each value adds 5 to their total over n values, so the mean rises by 5. The largest and smallest values both rise by 5, so their difference, the range, does not change. Example: 2, 4, 9 → 7, 9, 14.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
o: Power cuts in summer make life in a flat unbearable
The narrator's mother was the leader of the building
Mrs Baig had been a famous singer before she moved in
A long power cut unexpectedly brought the neighbours in a building closer
questions.x: Neighbours who barely knew each other spent the night together, and afterwards "Mrs Baig and my mother now drink tea together". "Famous" goes too far: she "had once been a singer".

questions.q: What did Mrs Baig bring to the roof?
questions.x: She "arrived with a plate of sliced mangoes". The torch and the water came with the narrator's family, and the mat was the Siddiquis'.

questions.q: It can be inferred that before that night, the families in the building:
o: met on the roof every week
questions.x: The narrator had said "perhaps ... ten words" to Mrs Baig in six years, and the children "had only ever nodded at each other". Nothing suggests dislike, only distance.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "improbable" most nearly means:
questions.x: A story about "a buffalo that had followed him home from a market" is hard to believe, so improbable means unlikely to be true. Nothing suggests it frightened anyone.

questions.q: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:
o: bitter, regretting that the night ended
quietly warm, noting a change that lasted
mocking, making fun of the neighbours
questions.x: Though "the building was itself again", the narrator notes, with warmth, the Sunday tea and the talks on the stairs. There is no regret or fear in the paragraph.

questions.q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: why lakes in Gilgit-Baltistan freeze harder than lakes elsewhere
how an unusual property of water lets fish survive under frozen lakes
how wax and water behave in the same way as they cool
why fish prefer very cold water to warm water
questions.x: The passage explains "an odd habit of water" and ends that this "quirk" "makes winter life in cold lakes possible". Wax is the contrast, not a match: water behaves like it "only down to about four degrees".

questions.q: What happens once the whole lake has cooled to about four degrees?
o: Water at the surface keeps cooling but stays on top because it is lighter
The coldest water sinks to the bottom and freezes there
Warm water rises from the lakebed and melts the surface
The whole lake turns to ice at the same moment
questions.x: The second paragraph says "After that, the surface water cools further but, being lighter, stays on top. It freezes there". Ice piling up on the lakebed is what would happen only if water behaved "like wax".

questions.q: The passage suggests that if ice were a good conductor of heat, the water beneath it would:
o: stay at a steady four degrees all winter
lose its warmth faster, so more of the lake might freeze
rise to the surface and melt the ice
become warmer than it is in summer
questions.x: The ice protects the water because it is "a poor conductor of heat", "slowing the loss of warmth from the water below"; a good conductor would let that warmth escape faster. A steady temperature is what the poor conductor provides, so it would no longer be assured.

questions.q: As used in the last paragraph, the word "quirk" most nearly means:
questions.x: The "quirk" is the "odd habit of water" described at the start, so it means an odd feature. It is not called a fault; it is what makes life possible.

questions.q: At the start of the third paragraph, the words "That lid" refer to:
o: the layer of water at about four degrees
the warmer water rising from below
the mud on the bed of the lake
the layer of ice formed on the surface of the lake
questions.x: The second paragraph ends with the surface water that "freezes there, forming a lid", and the third goes on: "Ice is a poor conductor". The four-degree water is what lies beneath the lid.
